fixes.explanation: Not even close, friend. Abijah, Judah's king, brings 400,000 chosen men, while Jeroboam, Israel's king, lines up 800,000 chosen and mighty men of valor. That's a full extra army on his side. Nobody calls that a tie by any math I know.

Abijah, Judah's king, stands on Mount Zemaraim and says, “Hear me, O Jeroboam and all Israel!” Jeroboam is Israel's king. So Abijah starts with a speech. Standing up high and talking to Jeroboam's 800,000 men takes some nerve, baker.

Abijah says Jeroboam son of Nebat, a servant of Solomon son of David, “…rose up and rebelled against his master.” Abijah is reading a man's work history out loud in front of 800,000 people, baker. That's the speech equivalent of pulling out a folder.

Abijah actually says it straight out. Jeroboam son of Nebat was a servant of Solomon son of David, and Abijah says Jeroboam “…rose up and rebelled against his master.” So this one is True, baker. Abijah is saying it to Jeroboam, Israel's king, in that very speech.

Abijah says they have with them “…the golden calves that Jeroboam made for you as gods.” Jeroboam is Israel's king, and Abijah, Judah's king, is calling out what he made. Gods that somebody made, baker. I stamp cookies all day, and nobody bows to them.

Silver's a shiny guess, friend, but this verse goes with gold. Abijah, Judah's king, says the army has with it “…the golden calves that Jeroboam made for you as gods.” Jeroboam is Israel's king. Golden calves, so the silver can wait for another day.

Abijah asks, “But did you not drive out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites?” So the priests of the LORD got pushed out. Abijah, Judah's king, brings it up in front of Jeroboam and all Israel.

It's the reverse, baker. Abijah, Judah's king, asks, “But did you not drive out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites?” Driving out and putting in charge don't land in the same spot. Not even close.
No land gifts in this speech. Abijah, Judah's king, asks, “But did you not drive out the priests of the LORD, the sons of Aaron, and the Levites?” They were driven out, baker, not given land.

Abijah, Judah's king, says, “…the LORD is our God. We have not forsaken Him…” He says it right after talking about the other side's priests. So he's drawing a line between Judah and Israel. I think he's proud of that line, baker.

Baal isn't named anywhere in this speech, baker. Abijah, Judah's king, says the priests present burnt offerings and fragrant incense “…to the LORD…” every morning and every evening. Morning, evening, morning, evening. My oven gets more breaks than that schedule, and it's all for the LORD.

Chasing isn't what he warns about, friend. Abijah, Judah's king, says to the children of Israel, “…do not fight against the LORD, the God of your fathers, for you will not succeed.” Notice who he names: the LORD, the God of their fathers, not Judah's army.

Jeroboam, Israel's king, “…had sent troops around to ambush from the rear…” so that “…while he was in front of Judah, the ambush was behind them.” So Judah has Jeroboam in front and an ambush behind, baker. Talk about a plot twist.

Nobody climbs the mountain in this verse. Jeroboam, Israel's king, “…had sent troops around to ambush from the rear…” So the troops went around to the rear of Judah, not up to Abijah, Judah's king. The ambush was behind Judah.

Jerusalem isn't the target in this verse. Jeroboam, Israel's king, “…had sent troops around to ambush from the rear…” The ambush was behind Judah, not at Jerusalem. Abijah is Judah's king, and the text puts the ambush behind his people.
When Judah discovers the battle is both before and behind them, “…they cried out to the LORD.” Surrounded on both sides, they call on the LORD. That's the move the text gives us, baker.
Surrender never comes up. When Judah finds the battle both before and behind them, “…they cried out to the LORD.” Jeroboam is Israel's king. The text gives them a cry to the LORD, not a surrender.
No shields get dropped in this verse. After the priests blow the trumpets, “…the men of Judah raised the battle cry.” That's a shout, baker, and the text says nothing about laying anything down.

The text doesn't give that as the reason. Abijah, Judah's king, had 400,000 men, and Jeroboam, Israel's king, had 800,000. What it says is “…the men of Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.” It's all about who they trusted, baker.

The text doesn't give surprise as the reason. Jeroboam, Israel's king, had sent troops to ambush from the rear, and Judah discovered the battle was both before and behind them. What it says is “…the men of Judah prevailed because they relied on the LORD, the God of their fathers.” So it was trust, baker.

Nice try with Joppa, baker, but it's not on the list. The text says Abijah, Judah's king, captured “Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, along with their villages.” He took them from Jeroboam, Israel's king. Bethel is the name that leads that list, and it's the one that fits.

Hebron sounds like a good guess, friend, but it's not in this verse. The text says Abijah, Judah's king, captured “Bethel, Jeshanah, and Ephron, along with their villages.” He took them from Jeroboam, Israel's king. Bethel is the first name on that list.

The text says, “Jeroboam did not again recover his power during the days of Abijah…” Jeroboam is Israel's king, and Abijah is Judah's king. So Jeroboam did not recover his power in Abijah's days, which makes this one False, baker.

The text says, “But Abijah grew strong…” Abijah is Judah's king. The verse goes on to say he married fourteen wives and became the father of twenty-two sons and sixteen daughters. That's a full house, baker.
The text says it right out: “But Abijah grew strong…” Abijah is Judah's king. So this one is True, baker. No shrinking in that verse.
